scholarly_monograph_synthesis.author_and_historical_context: According to the Georgian National Academy of Sciences ('Georgian Encyclopedia', Elguja Khintibidze), Shota Rustaveli ('Rustveli' in primary manuscripts) was a court poet of the Kingdom of Georgia at the turn of the 12th–13th centuries, composing the epic between c. 1189 and 1207 during the reign of Queen Tamar and her consort David Soslan. The prevailing scholarly consensus identifies him with Shota Rustaveli, the Royal Treasurer ('Mechurchletukhutsesi'), depicted in a 13th-century fresco between St. Maximus the Confessor and St. John of Damascus on a pillar of the Georgian Monastery of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, accompanied by the inscription 'God forgive Shota, the painter of this. Amen' and recorded in the monastery's synodikon ('agape' book).
scholarly_monograph_synthesis.title_semantics: In Old Georgian, 'vepkhi' ('ვეფხი') denoted a panther or leopard (as attested in medieval Georgian translations from Greek and Persian and 17th–18th century manuscript miniatures), whereas in modern Georgian it came to mean 'tiger'. The title 'Vepkhistkaosani' ('One Clad in a Panther's Skin') unites the central romantic pair in a single image: Tariel wears the panther's skin because the panther symbolizes his beloved Nestan-Darejan (' merciless as a leopard/panther', Stanza 19).
scholarly_monograph_synthesis.composition_and_poetics: As demonstrated by Zaza Khintibidze and Elguja Khintibidze, the poem's composition follows the classical Aristotelian model of Homeric unity ('Poetics', 1450b–1459b), which Rustaveli formulates theoretically in Stanzas 12–17 of the Prologue: narrating a vast overarching plot concisely ('grdzeli sitqva mokled itkmis') while developing key episodes in full detail and cutting off tributary episodes ('leksta grdzelta tkma da kheva') as soon as their function in the main plot is fulfilled.
scholarly_monograph_synthesis.historical_allegory_and_oriental_framewo: While Rustaveli frames the story as a 'Persian tale' with structural parallels to the Sanskrit 'Ramayana', Fakhruddin Gurgani's 'Vis and Ramin', and Nizami Ganjavi's 'Layla and Majnun', both the Arabian and Indian plotlines allegorize 12th-century Georgian court politics: King George III's unprecedented enthronement of his daughter Queen Tamar during his lifetime (paralleled by King Rostevan enthroning Tinatin in Arabia) versus the dynastic crisis of inviting a foreign prince as consort against the heir's wishes (paralleled by King Parsadan's attempt to marry Nestan-Darejan to the Khwarazmian prince in India, and hinting at the Demna Batonishvili dynastic conflict).
scholarly_monograph_synthesis.philosophy_and_ethics: Rustaveli synthesizes Biblical Christianity (Genesis, Psalms, Gospels, Pauline and Johannine Epistles), Patristics (St. Basil the Great, St. Gregory of Nyssa), Christian Neoplatonism (Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite and the 12th-century Georgian philosopher Ioane Petritsi), Plato ('Republic'/'Politeia', 'Symposium', 'Phaedrus', 'Gorgias'), and Aristotle ('Poetics', 'De Anima', 'Nicomachean Ethics'). Central to the poem is Aristotle's doctrine of the Golden Mean ('sashuali'): noble earthly love ('mijnuroba') is elevated as the ideal mean between otherworldly ascetic mysticism and base carnal lust ('sidzva'), while royal generosity ('siukhve') is the mean between prodigality and avarice.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Prologue (Introductory Quatrains)
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: The poet's invocation to the Creator God, panegyric dedication to Queen Tamar and David Soslan, self-identification as Rustveli, and two foundational theoretical treatises: the Theory of Poetry ('Shairoba', Stanzas 12–17) and the Theory of Chivalric Love ('Mijnuroba', Stanzas 20–31).
chapters_index.act_title: Act I: Arabia, The Royal Hunt & Quest for the Stranger Knight

location.desc: Realm of King Rostevan, Queen Tinatin, and Commander-in-Chief Avtandil.

chapters_index.key_maxim_ka: გრძელი სიტყვა მოკლედ ითქმის, შაირია ამად კარგი
chapters_index.key_maxim_en: A long word is said briefly; therefore is poetry good. (Stanza 12)

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Story of Rostevan, King of the Arabians
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Aging King Rostevan of Arabia, having no son, consults his viziers—who formulate the famous Georgian Renaissance maxim of gender equality in royal succession ('The lion's whelps are equal, be they female or male', Stanza 39)—and crowns his daughter Tinatin, instructing her in Aristotelian-Christian royal generosity ('What you give away is yours; what you keep is lost', Stanza 50). At the royal banquet, Commander-in-Chief Avtandil challenges Rostevan to an archery hunting contest.
chapters_index.act_title: Act I: Arabia, The Royal Hunt & Quest for the Stranger Knight

location.desc: Realm of King Rostevan, Queen Tinatin, and Commander-in-Chief Avtandil.

chapters_index.key_maxim_ka: ლეკვი ლომისა სწორია, ძუ იყოს, თუნდა ხვადია
chapters_index.key_maxim_en: The lion's whelps are equal, be they female or male. (Stanza 39)

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Hunting of King Rostevan and Avtandil
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Rostevan and Avtandil conduct a grand royal battue hunt across the plain, slaying 2,000 beasts (100 score) between them; Avtandil wins by 20 beasts without missing a single shot, and Rostevan rejoices in his foster-son's martial perfection.
chapters_index.act_title: Act I: Arabia, The Royal Hunt & Quest for the Stranger Knight

chapters_index.key_maxim_en: What you give away is yours; what you keep is lost! (Stanza 50)

chapters_index.chapter_title_ka: ნახვა არაბთა მეფისაგან მის ყმისა ვეფხის-ტყაოსნისა
chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Seeing by the King of the Arabians of the Knight Clad in the Panther's Skin
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Resting by a stream after the hunt, Rostevan and Avtandil behold a weeping stranger knight clad in a panther's skin (Tariel). Lost in sorrow, the knight ignores Rostevan's envoys, effortlessly routs the royal guards when they attempt to seize him, and vanishes without a trace. Queen Tinatin counsels her grieving father with Christian-Neoplatonic theology ('Why should the Creator of good make evil?', Stanza 113) and advises sending searchers across the earth.
chapters_index.act_title: Act I: Arabia, The Royal Hunt & Quest for the Stranger Knight

location.desc: Where Rostevan and Avtandil first behold the weeping Knight in the Panther's Skin.

chapters_index.key_maxim_ka: კაცმან საქმე მოიგვაროს, ვეჭვ, ჭმუნვასა ესე სჯობდეს
chapters_index.key_maxim_en: Let a man contrive a deed; I think this is better than grieving. (Stanza 114)

chapters_index.chapter_title_ka: თინათინისაგან ავთანდილის გაგზავნა მის ყმის საძებრად
chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Tinatin Sends Avtandil in Quest of the Knight
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Queen Tinatin summons Avtandil to their first private meeting, acknowledges his hidden courtly love for her, and commands him as her vassal and lover ('First thou art a knight... second, thou art my lover', Stanza 130) to search for the Knight in the Panther's Skin for three years, swearing an oath to wed none but Avtandil. Avtandil confides in his loyal retainer Shermadin and appoints him regent of his domain.
chapters_index.act_title: Act I: Arabia, The Royal Hunt & Quest for the Stranger Knight

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Letter of Avtandil to his Vassals
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Avtandil writes an official charter to his nobles and troops instructing them to obey Shermadin as himself during his three-year absence, then rides out from his frontier city under the pretext of a border expedition before slipping away alone.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Departure of Avtandil in Quest of the Knight
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Avtandil wanders across the world for two years and nine months seeking news of the stranger knight. Just as his three-year term is nearly spent, he meets three Khatavian brothers in the wilderness whose youngest brother was struck down with a whip by the Knight in the Panther's Skin, and follows their directions to Tariel's cliffside cave.

chapters_index.key_maxim_ka: ვარდსა უკითხავს: ეკალო, ვინ დაგამსგავსა ლალებსა?
chapters_index.key_maxim_en: The rose asked the thorn: who made thee like rubies?

chapters_index.chapter_title_ka: ამბავი ავთანდილისა, ასმათს რომ ეუბნების ქვაბშიგან
chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Story of Avtandil Speaking with Asmat in the Cave
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: At the cave hidden among rocks and reeds, Avtandil encounters the weeping maidservant Asmat. When she initially mistakes him for an enemy and refuses to speak, Avtandil overcomes her distrust by invoking the name of love ('mijnuroba'), persuading her to shelter him and introduce him to Tariel.

chapters_index.key_maxim_ka: მიჯნურობა არის ტურფა, საცოდნელად ძნელი გვარი
chapters_index.key_maxim_en: Chivalric love is fair, a kind hard to know.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Meeting of Tariel and Avtandil
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Tariel returns to the cave and Asmat brings out Avtandil. Captivated at first sight by each other's spiritual and physical nobility, the two knights embrace, weep together, and swear eternal brotherhood, after which Avtandil explains how King Rostevan and Queen Tinatin sent him on his quest.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Telling of his Tale by Tariel when he First Told it to Avtandil
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Tariel begins narrating his life story: how his father Saridan, King of one-seventh of India, voluntarily united his realm with King Parsadan of the other six kingdoms (reflecting Rustaveli's ideal of a centralized monarchy) in exchange for the office of Amirbar (Commander-in-Chief and Grand Admiral), and how Tariel was raised as heir by the childless King Parsadan and Queen until the birth of Princess Nestan-Darejan.
chapters_index.act_title: Act II: Tariel's Chronicle of India, Love & Loss

location.desc: Homeland of King Parsadan, Princess Nestan-Darejan, and Amirbar Tariel.

chapters_index.key_maxim_en: A sweetly speaking tongue brings a snake out from its lair.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Tale of Tariel's Falling in Love when he First Fell in Love
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: After the death of his father Saridan, Tariel inherits the office of Amirbar. Accompanying King Parsadan to Nestan-Darejan's secluded pavilion to deliver partridges, Tariel glimpses Nestan-Darejan when Asmat lifts the curtain and immediately falls unconscious for three days, struck by consuming love (a motif paralleling Gurgani's 'Vis and Ramin').

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Counsel Concerning the Marriage of Nestan-Darejan
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: King Parsadan and the Queen summon Tariel to a royal council and announce their decision to bring the son of the Shah of Khwarazm to marry Nestan-Darejan and rule India. Bound by feudal etiquette and fear of exposing his secret love, Tariel is forced to give outward consent while his heart breaks.
chapters_index.act_title: Act II: Tariel's Chronicle of India, Love & Loss

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Counsel and Resolution of Tariel and Nestan-Darejan
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Tariel meets an indignant Nestan-Darejan, who condemns her parents' decision to hand the Indian throne to a foreign Khwarazmian prince rather than to Tariel, the rightful hereditary claimant and her sworn betrothed. Rejecting court intrigue, they resolve that Tariel will slay the bridegroom upon arrival and demand justice from King Parsadan (allegorizing 12th-century Georgian royal marriage debates).

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Arrival of the Khwarazmsha's Son in India for the Wedding and his Slaying by Tariel
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: When the Khwarazmian prince arrives and pitches his tents, Tariel rides at night with a hundred men, enters the tent, and slays the bridegroom cleanly without shedding the blood of his sleeping retinue, then fortifies himself in his city and sends word to King Parsadan that he will never allow a foreign prince to usurp the Indian throne.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Tariel Hears Tidings of the Loss of Nestan-Darejan
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Furious, King Parsadan blames his sister Davar (a sorceress who raised Nestan-Darejan) and swears to kill her. Davar beats Nestan-Darejan for instigating the slaying, puts her in an ark carried by two black sorcerer slaves into the sea, and commits suicide. Learning this from the bleeding Asmat, Tariel sets out in desperate search of Nestan.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Story of Nuradin Pridon when Tariel Met him
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: After searching for a year until his retinue perishes from exhaustion, Tariel (accompanied only by Asmat and three retainers) meets the wounded knight-king Nuradin Pridon of Mulghazanzar on the seashore, betrayed by his cousins over a hunting island. Struck by Pridon's heroic spirit, Tariel swears brotherhood with him.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Tariel's Aid to Pridon
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Tariel boards the enemy ships single-handedly, routs Pridon's cousins on sea and land, and restores Pridon to his throne in Mulghazanzar.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Pridon Tells Tariel Tidings of Nestan-Darejan
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Pridon recounts how he once saw from a headland two black slaves bring a moon-like maiden out of a chest on a boat before another ship carried her away. When Pridon's mariners cannot find her, Tariel retreats to the wilderness cave conquered from the Devis, where Asmat tends him. Deeply moved, Avtandil pledges to report back to Tinatin in Arabia and return within two months to help Tariel find Nestan-Darejan.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Story of Avtandil's Return to Arabia
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Avtandil rides back to Arabia, is joyfully welcomed by Shermadin and King Rostevan, and recounts Tariel's full story to Queen Tinatin, who praises his fidelity and urges him to fulfill his oath to return and aid his sworn brother.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Testament of Avtandil to King Rostevan
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: The ethical and philosophical pinnacle of the epic (Stanzas 788–808): Avtandil writes his testament to King Rostevan, justifying his departure through Plato ('Falsehood and two-facedness injure the body, then the soul', Stanza 789), Christian Neoplatonism ('union with the choir of heavenly choirs', Stanza 790), the Apostles ('Love exalts us', Stanza 791), chivalric honor ('Better a glorious death than a shameful life', Stanza 800), and charitable emancipation of his slaves and distribution of his wealth to the poor, orphans, hospices, and bridge-building.

Avtandil revives him and delivers a masterful philosophical discourse on stoic endurance and active reason ('If a wise man abandons wisdom, how shall he prosper?', Stanza 882), persuading Tariel to mount his horse.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Tariel's Telling of the Slaying of the Lion and the Panther
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Tariel recounts one of the poem's most famous symbolic episodes: he watched a lion and a female panther play together like lovers until they quarreled; indignant at the lion for striking the female, Tariel slew the lion with his sword and tried to embrace the panther for reminding him of Nestan-Darejan, but when the panther bit and clawed him, he hurled her down in grief.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Letter of Nestan-Darejan to her Beloved
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: One of the lyrical masterpieces of Georgian literature (Stanzas 1292–1317): Nestan-Darejan writes to Tariel expressing her undying love, sending a fringe cut from the Khatavian veil he gave her, warning him not to rush into certain death at Kadjeti, and uttering her famous prayer of spiritual transcendence ('Entrust me to God, perchance He will free me from the travail of the world... grant me wings that I may fly', Stanza 1304).

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Departure of Avtandil from Gulansharo and his Meeting with Tariel
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Avtandil sails from Gulansharo, rides joyously to the cave, finds Tariel standing by the reeds with a freshly slain lion, and presents Nestan-Darejan's letter and veil token. After reviving the overwhelmed Tariel, they open the sealed treasure-chambers of the cave and arm themselves with invulnerable Kadji-forged armor and swords.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Counsel of Avtandil
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Avtandil objects that clanking armor would alert the guards on a rope, and proposes instead to enter the fortress alone disguised as a merchant with weapons concealed on a mule, then cut down the gate-guards from within.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Counsel of Tariel (and the Storming of Kadjeti)
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Tariel rejects leaving either sworn brother out of the battle or letting Nestan see him hang back, proposing instead to divide the 300 men into three hundred-man detachments led by himself, Avtandil, and Pridon to charge the three gates simultaneously at dawn. Executing Tariel's plan with superhuman valor ('those three are covered by the seven planets with a column of light'), they storm Kadjeti, rout the 10,000 defenders, and liberate Nestan-Darejan.

chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: The three sworn brothers, Nestan-Darejan, and Asmat return to the cave, load the remaining treasures of the Devis, and travel to Arabia. Tariel sends Asmat ahead and personally intercedes with King Rostevan to pardon Avtandil for his secret departure and bless Avtandil's marriage to Queen Tinatin.

chapters_index.chapter_title_en: Wedding of Tariel and Nestan-Darejan (in India)
chapters_index.chapter_expert_explanation_en: Tariel and Nestan-Darejan are crowned King and Queen of all seven kingdoms of India, rewarding the faithful Asmat with one-seventh of India as her own principality and establishing a golden age of justice, mercy, and mutual aid with Avtandil in Arabia and Pridon in Mulghazanzar ('Even the goat and the wolf fed together').
